t.en: A new symbol, ∃, reads “there exists”: ∃x. P(x) says at least one thing x in the world satisfies P.

First build a sentence as a formula; when it is wrong, the checker may show a small world where it and the target differ. Then someone else has translated the sentence too, and it is your turn to show with a world that they got it wrong.

brief.en: Build this sentence as a formula from the parts below.

hint.en: “Some bird flies”: there is a thing x that is a bird and flies.
Writing “x is a bird → x flies” is made true by anything at all that is not a bird.

brief.en: You built this sentence as a formula; this is someone else’s. Build a world where the two differ in truth.

hint.en: What if the world holds no bird at all?

t.en: In propositional logic, whether a sentence is true depends on the row of the truth table. In first-order logic it depends on the world: how many things there are, what each is and how they relate.

Above are your translation and someone else’s. To show theirs is wrong, build a world where the two differ: choose below how many things there are, then tap what holds of each. A run marks above whether each translation is true in this world.
